subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: escalating to compliance if unresolved [Revision]
passage:
Thursday night.
I talked to Tarun today, like I said I would. Calmly, with the dates: the same figures being changed before every month-end review. Tarun waved a hand. "Everyone does it. Don't make trouble." My cheeks were burning as I left the room.
I sat in the stairwell for a while. I wanted to vent in the team chat, or post something where people could see. I didn't. That feels like a different story from the one I want to tell.
Instead, I wrote a plain message to the compliance office: what I saw, on which dates, and that I raised it with Tarun first. Sent at 6:10. An acknowledgement with a reference number came within the hour.
Now I wait. I'm scared, but calm.
— Sarika

qa.q: What time did Sarika send the note to the compliance team?
What was Sarika feeling after Tarun waved the concern away?
qa.a: Sarika felt embarrassed and shaken, with burning cheeks, and tempted to vent publicly.

qa.q: What could Sarika do if the compliance team does not respond?
qa.a: Sarika could quote the reference number and ask for an update, or use any other official channel the policy names.

qa.q: How might Tarun see Sarika's note to compliance?
qa.a: Tarun may feel surprised and worried that the concern went further, since Tarun had told Sarika not to make trouble.

grounding: The diary shows an employee whose manager dismisses a concern, so the employee sends a written note to the compliance team through the official process, without gossip.

Kishore: sent at 6.12 pm. got an auto-reply with a case number
Indu: how do you feel
Kishore: sick in the stomach honestly. but also like I can sleep tonight

subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
subtype: Approach: escalating to compliance if unresolved [Revision]
passage:
At the microfinance branch in Raichur, Siddharth had noticed loan files for village women whose signatures looked identical. He showed the branch manager, Bhavna, three files side by side. She waved a hand. 'Field staff are rushing. Don't make a fuss over paperwork.'
That night, at the lodge where he rented a room, he read the ethics section of the staff handbook by torchlight during a power cut. If the manager does not act, write to compliance at head office. He did not ring his friends at other branches. He did not post anything anywhere.
Next morning, before the bus came, he wrote a two-page letter: file numbers, dates, what he had shown Bhavna and what she said. He sent it by registered post and emailed a scanned copy to the compliance address. Then he went to work as usual.

qa.q: Where did Siddharth read the ethics section?
qa.a: At the lodge where he rented a room, by torchlight during a power cut.

qa.q: What might Siddharth have been worried about before writing?
qa.a: He was probably uneasy about going over Bhavna's head, and worried that the women's names were being misused on loans.

qa.q: Why was writing to compliance better than calling friends at other branches?
qa.a: It follows the official process and keeps the facts clean, while calls to friends could turn into gossip and warn the wrong people.

qa.q: How might the village women named in the files be affected?
qa.a: If the signatures were faked, they could be held responsible for loans they never took, so the escalation may protect them.

grounding: It shows an employee escalating in writing to compliance after the manager dismisses the issue, avoiding gossip or social media.
